lessons.title: café — coffee, and a place to drink it
lessons.gloss: coffee / a café — one useful noun before the polite request that follows

segments.text: Before you can make a polite request, you need one small thing to request. Café gives you a useful noun and lets the written accent do a job you already understand.
Say ca-FÉ. A vowel-final word would normally stress the second-to-last syllable, so the acute accent records the unexpected final stress.

Spanish café came through Italian caffè and Turkish kahve from Arabic qahwah. English coffee reached the same travelling word by a different European route. The drink and the word both crossed languages.
Café can name the drink or the place, just as English coffee and café divide those jobs. It is masculine: el café.

segments.instruction: the route — “qahwah becomes kahve becomes caffè becomes café”
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the route — “qahwah → kahve → caffè → café”]

segments.text: Where does the stress fall? (On the final é.) Why is the accent written? (It overrides the usual vowel-final stress.) What route carried the word into Spanish? (Arabic qahwah becomes Turkish kahve becomes Italian caffè becomes Spanish café.)
You can already thank (gracias) and reply (de nada). The third courtesy completes the set: por favor, "please" — literally "for [a] favour." You're asking someone to do you a kindness.
r-tap — one soft tapped r in por and favor.
v-b — Spanish v and b sound identical (a soft b): favor ≈ fah-BOR. (So favor and English favour look alike and the v even sounds like the b you'd hear in "harbour.")

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the phrase

segments.text: por = "for / through / by," from Latin prō ("for, on behalf of") — the same pro- in English pronoun, propose, protect.
favor = "a favour, goodwill," from Latin favēre, "to be favourable to, to support." It's the very word English borrowed: favour, favorite, favorable, favouritism.

So por favor literally says “for a favour” — [do this] as a kindness to me. English favour, favorite, and favorable keep the same Latin family visible without asking you to learn another language's formula.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the courtesy set is complete

segments.text: You now hold the three pillars of politeness:
por favor — please (asking).
gracias — thank you (receiving).
de nada — you're welcome (replying).

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "favor" then English "favour, favorite" — one family]

segments.text: What does por favor literally mean? ("For a favour.") What Latin verb is favor from, and its English cousins? (favēre — favour, favorite, favorable.) Which three-word courtesy loop do you now own? (Por favor becomes gracias becomes de nada.) Next: your first regular verb — hablar, “to speak.”

lessons.title: hablar — "to speak," and the engine of Spanish sentences
lessons.gloss: to speak / to talk (your first regular -ar verb)

needs: your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud
waitUntilStopped: Grammar Lens: the -ar present tense (the big one)
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Grammar Lens: the -ar present tense (the big one) until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Fixed phrases got you this far. Hablar (“to speak”) gives you a reusable singular -ar pattern. One ending swap says “I speak,” asks a friend, or addresses someone formally.
silent-h — the h is completely silent: hablar = ah-BLAR. (Spanish h never makes a sound.)
v-b — the b is a soft b; hablo = AH-bloh.

hablar comes from Latin fābulārī, "to chat, to tell tales" — from fābula, "a story." So to speak, in Spanish, is at root to tell stories. That fābula is thoroughly English: fable, fabulous ("story-like"), confabulate, and ineffable ("un-speak-able").

The initial Latin f- weakened and eventually disappeared in this word, leaving the written but silent Spanish h-. The single path you need today is fābulārī becomes hablar; later words will let you test how broadly the same historical pattern reaches.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the -ar present tense (the big one)

segments.text: Hablar belongs to the -ar family. To conjugate the three singular forms you need now, drop -ar and add the ending for the person:

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 3 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: person, ending, hablar, which gives:, meaning. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
The -o ending already says “I,” so Spanish normally leaves the subject pronoun unstated. That is pro-drop: hablo is a complete “I speak.”
This same template fits every regular -ar verb. Next you'll snap two more verbs straight into it.

segments.instruction: the pattern — “hablo, hablas, habla” (I / tú / usted)
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the pattern — “hablo, hablas, habla” (I / tú / usted)]

segments.instruction: "hablar" then English "fable, fabulous, ineffable" — the fābula root
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "hablar" then English "fable, fabulous, ineffable" — the *fābula* root]

segments.text: What Latin word is hablar from, and what English word shares it? (fābulārī from fābula — fable.) What happened to its initial Latin f-? (It weakened away, leaving silent Spanish h-.) How do you say “I speak,” and why is no subject pronoun required? (Hablo — the -o ending carries “I.”) Next: trabajar, “to work.”

lessons.title: trabajar — "to work," and it once meant torture
lessons.gloss: to work (a second -ar verb — same pattern)

segments.text: A second -ar verb — snap it into the exact template you just learned. And trabajar has the darkest, best etymology in this chapter: it began as a word for torture, and it's the secret origin of English travel.
j-jota — the j is a raspy h-from-the-throat (the jota): trabajar = tra-ba-HAR.
r-tap, b-soft — tapped r, soft b.
trabajar comes from Vulgar Latin tripaliāre, "to torture" — from tripalium, a Roman instrument of torture made of three stakes (tri- "three" + pālus "stake," the root of English pale and impale).
The chain of meaning is grimly logical: torture becomes torment / suffering becomes hard toil becomes just work. And English took the very same word down a parallel road:
travail — painful, laborious effort (and the pains of childbirth).
travel — yes: journeying was once such an ordeal that "travail" (toil) became travel (to make a journey). Every time you travel, you're etymologically being tortured.
So even plain trabajo, “I work,” hides the old idea of toil as torment — a dark little joke inside an everyday verb.
Drop -ar, add the ending — identical to hablar:

utterances: person: I (ending carries the subject). form: trabajo. meaning: I work.
person: tú. form: trabajas. meaning: you work.
person: usted. form: trabaja. meaning: you (formal) work.

segments.text: Notice you didn't learn a new ending — that's the point. One template, every regular -ar verb.

segments.instruction: "trabajo, trabajas, trabaja" — same endings as hablo/hablas/habla
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "trabajo, trabajas, trabaja" — same endings as *hablo/hablas/habla*]

segments.instruction: "trabajar" becomes travail becomes travel — torture became a journey
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "trabajar" → travail → travel — torture became a journey]

segments.text: What did trabajar originally mean, and from what device? ("To torture," from tripalium, a three-stake tool.) What two English words come from the same root? (Travail and travel.) How do you say "I work"? (Trabajo — same -o ending.) Next: estudiar, "to study."

lessons.title: estudiar — "to study," and the eagerness inside it
lessons.gloss: to study (a third -ar verb — the pattern is automatic now)

segments.text: Your third -ar verb. By now the pattern should feel automatic — that's exactly what we want. estudiar also hides a nicer feeling than the classroom suggests: at root it means eagerness.
st-no-e — Spanish props up st- with an e: es-tudiar (the same reflex behind estar, España, escuela). es-too-DYAR.
diphthong-io — the -iar glides: es-too-DYAR.

estudiar comes from Latin studēre, "to be eager, to apply oneself zealously." A studium was zeal, enthusiasm, devotion — only later "study." So to study is, at heart, to throw yourself eagerly at something.
That studēre is everywhere in English:
student — literally "one who is eager."
studio, studious, study — the place, the trait, the act.
Italian studio and the musical studio keep the "devoted practice" sense.
So Estudio español is "I devote myself eagerly to Spanish" — a nicer picture than mere schoolwork.
Drop -ar, add the ending — for the third time:

utterances: person: I (ending carries the subject). form: estudio. meaning: I study.
person: tú. form: estudias. meaning: you study.
person: usted. form: estudia. meaning: you (formal) study.

segments.text: Three verbs, one pattern: hablo, trabajo, estudio. The singular regular -ar present is now reusable rather than memorized verb by verb.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "estudio, estudias, estudia" — the now-familiar endings]

segments.text: What did studēre originally mean? ("To be eager / apply oneself.") Its English cousins? (Student, studio, studious.) Say "I study" — and notice it uses the same -o as hablo and trabajo. (Estudio.) Next: put a verb and a noun together into your first real sentence.

lessons.title: Hablo español — your first real sentence
lessons.gloss: "I speak Spanish" — your first full sentence (español = Spanish)

segments.text: This is the moment the course has been building to: you take a verb you conjugated and a noun, and make a sentence nobody handed you pre-assembled. Hablo español — "I speak Spanish."

español = "Spanish" (the language, and a Spaniard), from Hispania, the Roman name for the Iberian peninsula. The path Hispania becomes hispaniolus becomes español wore the word down, and — look — the ñ is back, exactly the doubled-n-under- a-tilde you met in the writing lesson (Hispaniolus becomes españ-ol). Say it es-pa-NYOL.
(English "Spanish," "Hispanic," and "Hispania" are all the same root — and, fittingly, español itself may trace back through Latin to a Phoenician name for the coast, "land of hyraxes / rabbits.")

blocks.title: What you've built — the sentence assembled

segments.text: Snap two things you already own together:
Hablo (I speak, from hablar) + español (Spanish) = Hablo español.
That's it — a complete, grammatical Spanish sentence. Note what's not there:
No separate subject word. The -o of hablo already says “I,” reusing the pro-drop pattern from the previous lesson.
No "the" or "a." Languages are bare: hablo español, not "el español."
Now swap the pieces and watch it generate:
Estudio español. — “I study Spanish.”
Trabajo. — “I work.”
¿Hablas español? — “Do you speak Spanish?” (reuse the ¿? from the writing lesson).

segments.instruction: ask it — "¿Hablas español?" (raise the pitch, ¿ opens the question)
segments.source: [YOU SAY: ask it — "¿Hablas español?" (raise the pitch, ¿ opens the question)]

segments.text: Where does español come from, and what letter does its ending bring back? (Hispania; the ñ.) In Hablo español, why is there no separate subject word and no “the”? (The -o ending carries “I”; languages take no article.) You just built your first sentence from parts — that's the whole game from here. Next: practice.

lessons.title: Practice — making sentences with -ar verbs
lessons.gloss: your first sentences — the -ar present tense in action

segments.text: A milestone chapter: for the first time you're not reciting fixed phrases, you're building sentences from a pattern. Drill the three verbs through the endings until hablo / hablas / habla is automatic.
Run each verb through the three singular jobs you know: the ending alone for I becomes tú becomes usted:
hablar: hablo, hablas, habla.
trabajar: trabajo, trabajas, trabaja.
estudiar: estudio, estudias, estudia.
Same three endings (-o / -as / -a) every time — that's the whole regular -ar present, singular.
— ¿Hablas español? — Hablo español. — ¿Estudias español? — Estudio español. — Café, por favor. — ¡Gracias! — De nada.
por favor — please ( from "for a favour"), completing gracias / de nada / por favor.
the singular regular -ar pattern — drop -ar, add -o / -as / -a: the template behind hablar, trabajar, and estudiar.
hablar ( from fābula, fable; the f becomes h law), trabajar ( from tripalium, torture becomes travail/travel), estudiar ( from studēre, eagerness becomes student).
Hablo español — your first self-assembled sentence (pro-drop, no article).

What are the three singular -ar endings? (-o / -as / -a.) Give the “I” form of all three verbs. (Hablo, trabajo, estudio.) Why does Hablo español need no separate subject word? (The -o carries “I.”) You can now generate sentences — the course stops handing you phrases and starts handing you rules. Next chapter adds the -er/-ir verb families.
